data.source_title: Effects of computerized prescriber order entry on pharmacy order-processing time
data.locator: Methods and Results; composition-to-pharmacist-verification and pharmacy-receipt-to-verification intervals
data.source_period: Before/after CPOE implementation; study period dates not reported in abstract (published 2009)
data.quantity: Mean time from prescriber composition to pharmacist verification
data.source_evidence_basis: An observational before/after study reports mean composition-to-verification time fell from 115 to 3 minutes after CPOE. The abstract also reports pharmacy-receipt-to-verification time fell from 31 to 3 minutes.
data.limitations: Single hospital and historical workflow comparison; implementation context and other changes may affect the comparison. Verification time does not measure dispensing, delivery, first administration, or current RWJ performance.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Represent order transmission and pharmacist verification as explicit timed stages, with an optional CPOE-era comparison scenario only when clearly labeled historical external evidence. Do not use the reported mean as an RWJ service-time distribution.

data.source_title: Effects of computerized prescriber order entry on pharmacy order-processing time
data.locator: Methods and Results; pharmacy receipt to pharmacist verification interval
data.source_period: Before/after CPOE implementation; study period dates not reported in abstract (published 2009)
data.source_n: 2,988 orders overall (1,488 pre, 1,500 post); sub-group counts not reported in abstract
data.source_evidence_basis: The reported interval begins when pharmacy receives an order and ends at pharmacist verification; it shortened from 31 minutes before CPOE to 3 minutes after CPOE in this hospital.
data.limitations: This measure ends at verification. It omits preparation/dispensing, transport to the nursing unit, administration readiness, medication availability, and bedside administration.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Keep verification completion separate from medication prepared, delivered, and administered states. Treat the source values as a historical external comparison, not a local baseline or service-time distribution.
